The dogmatic stabilization of the Immaterial Object of Consumption requires an additional step of applicational condensation. It is not enough that the previously constructed parameters be conceptually consistent. They must be able to circulate in a sufficiently dense, precise and citable form, capable of sustaining legal argument in diverse institutional settings. Whenever a dogmatic construction seeks to guide complaints, decisions, legal opinions, administrative filings and protection routines, it must offer operable language without sacrificing theoretical density or turning into an empty formula. It is at this point that the parameters take the form of operational statements, which do not replace legal reasoning with ready-made formulas, but prevent the incidence of the IOC from depending, in each new conflict, on an exhaustive return to the reconstructive itinerary that grounded its elaboration.

The statements should not be read as a horizontal inventory of concepts. Their function is to organize a staggered decision sequence, in which each parameter prepares the incidence of the <1>p. 717</1> next one and limits the field of interpretive variation of the subsequent step. One starts from the qualification of the object and of the enjoyment regime, without which the rest of the analysis becomes disorganized. Next, semiotic vulnerability comes into play as a mechanism of governance of meaning and of the intelligibility of the bond. Only then do the duties of information and advertising become legible, in a dogmatically useful key, understood as structural forms of organizing expectation, choice and contestation. From this core, the standards that structure the institutional controllability of the conflict come into play. Open auditability, functional value equivalence, abusive teleology and the rational distribution of evidentiary burdens operate as criteria of verification, containment and attribution. Reconciliation with intellectual property and the primacy of functional restoration appear, at the end, as necessary operational closures, defining, on the one hand, the limit of private exclusivity in the face of consumer-law protection and, on the other, the legally adequate form of response to the conflict.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption requires a framing instrument capable of reducing the institutional cost of translation between the complexity of the governed ecosystem and the legal response required in the concrete case. This requirement does not stem from a didactic concern in a weak sense, but from the need to make operable, in a decisional key, a dogmatic grammar built precisely to confront bonds in which enjoyment is administered by private architecture, ordinary mutability, structural opacity and asymmetric mechanisms of sanction, visibility and contestation. When the consumer's experience is produced, modulated and narrated by the supplier itself, the interpreter's difficulty lies not only in understanding the environment, but in converting that understanding into a legally controllable framing.

For this reason, the present systematization works as a reference tool. Its usefulness lies not in artificially simplifying the object, but in organizing, in a manageable way, the passage between governance mechanism, supply duty, minimum evidentiary requirement, legal qualification and possible institutional consequence. The framework operates through cumulative filters. One starts from the identification of the IOC and of the governed enjoyment regime. Next, semiotic vulnerability is qualified and, as the case may be, structural opacity, relevant mutability and governance by sanction are verified. Open auditability and functional value <1>p. 743</1> equivalence operate as transversal filters, bearing upon different forms of conflict. Only then does one proceed to the legal qualification of the dispute, without prejudice to cumulation when the same arrangement reveals, simultaneously, relevant inadequacy of supply and repeated exploitation of vulnerability.

The underlying logic remains the same. In continuous digital services, the dispute does not enter the system as raw fact. It already arrives traversed by regimes of perception, expectation and intelligibility produced by the supplier. That is why the reconstruction of the decisional experience occupies a central position. Without it, evidence tends to be replaced by a cultural impression about technology, and the legal response degrades into intuitive deference or generic hostility toward the digital. The function of the framework is precisely to avoid this drift, providing a framing grammar that makes it possible to operate the CDC and to reconcile intellectual property without requiring total technical mastery of the ecosystem and without accepting complexity as an alibi for non-accountability.
The following framing blocks may then be established:
a) governed enjoyment regime and incidence of the IOC;

Whenever the utility consumed depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and mutable by private governance, with impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating of the experience, the field of incidence of the IOC will be configured. The corresponding supply duty is to ensure enjoyment that is functionally accessible, intelligible and preserved within the limits of the legitimate mutability of the environment. The minimum required evidence falls on the demonstration of the structural dependence of the utility on the governed ecosystem, of the way the experience is made available and of the consumer's concrete position in the bond. The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC, without the service dimension of the bond displacing the control of enjoyment as the core of supply. The possible institutional consequence consists in opening the subsequent filters of the regime, preventing the dispute from being neutralized by the claim of mere service provision or of simple formal licensing.
b) semiotic vulnerability and governance of meaning;

<1>p. 744</1> Whenever expectation, perception of value, risk assessment or capacity for contestation depend on signs, interfaces, flows and informational trails controlled by the supplier, there will be legally relevant semiotic vulnerability. The corresponding duty is not to organize the experience through a structural asymmetry of meaning incompatible with good faith, transparency and legibility of enjoyment. The minimum required evidence involves reconstruction of the user journey, of the informational architecture of the environment, of communicational saliences, of the paths of understanding and of the records available to reconstitute the formation of expectation. The possible legal qualification may support an abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness by ambiguity or relevant omission and, when articulated with other elements, grounds for dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof. The institutional consequence consists in bringing the conflict back to the governance of the environment, avoiding moralization of the consumer's conduct and allowing the incidence of reinforced duties of information, advertising and evidence.
c) inadequate information as functional opacity;

Whenever the platform replaces legibility with textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmentation of informational trajectories or merely performative transparency, there will be inadequacy of the duty to inform. The corresponding supply duty is to provide information that is materially adequate, useful for the decision and verifiable at a later moment of dispute. The minimum required evidence requires identifying what was shown, at what moment, with what salience, through which channels and to what extent this organization allowed the consumer to understand what was legally relevant to adhere, remain or react. The legal qualification tends to operate as an informational quality defect of supply, an abusive practice by functional obscuring and, as the case may be, support for the invalidity of clauses or of limitations incompatible with the legitimately formed expectation. The possible institutional consequence includes a duty to correct the communicational arrangement, reinforcement of useful transparency, disclosure orders and restoration of enjoyment affected by decisional opacity.
d) advertising and offer as controllable management of expectation;

Whenever enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences, advertising will <1>p. 745</1> materially integrate the offer. The corresponding supply duty is to ensure correspondence between promise, announced value, concealed costs and the experience actually made available under administered mutability. The minimum required evidence involves reconstruction of the promotional environment, of the communication pieces, of symbolic saliences, of the context of presentation of the object and of the relation between prior promise and subsequent enjoyment. The legal qualification may fall on misleading or abusive advertising, binding offer, abusive practice by administered ambiguity and, when articulated with a broader exploitative program, an element of abusive teleology. The possible institutional consequence encompasses correction of the offer, functional restoration, injunctive relief over the communication and, as the case may be, invalidation of promotional strategies incompatible with the real experience delivered.
e) structural opacity and open auditability;

Whenever relevant changes in access, performance, utility, operating rule or sanction bear upon enjoyment without preservation of minimum trails of institutional reconstruction, there will be a violation of the open auditability parameter. The corresponding supply duty is to maintain minimum verifiability over what was changed, when it was changed, on what grounds it was justified and what functionally relevant effects it produced.

The minimum required evidence consists of essential logs, history of relevant versions, sanction records, minimum operational justifications, context data and delimited technical elements sufficient to make the dispute cognizable. The possible legal qualification may take the form of an abusive practice by immunizing opacity, inadequacy of the supply regime and reinforcement of the duty of evidentiary cooperation, without prejudice to other combined incidences. The institutional consequence includes orders for preservation and disclosure of records, delimited expert examination, presumptions unfavorable to the supplier and control of the lawfulness of the change or sanction based on minimum institutional intelligibility.
f) relevant mutability and functional value equivalence;

Whenever the platform alters the experience so as to degrade, empty or substantially divert the function that justified the acquisition, there will be a rupture of functional value equivalence. The corresponding supply duty is to preserve, in substantial terms, the functional, relational and, when legally relevant, symbolic role of the object in the consumer's experience. The minimum required evidence requires demonstration of the utility <1>p. 746</1> previously incorporated into the bond, of the change that occurred, of the concrete functional impact of the alteration and of the insufficiency of any restoration offered. The possible legal qualification tends to fall on a quality defect of the product or service, relevant inadequacy of supply and, if there is coordinated exploitation of mutability, an additional element of abusive practice or abusive teleology. The possible institutional consequence prioritizes functional restoration, technical reversal when feasible, equivalent substitution and correction of the form of updating, instead of mere automatic monetization of the loss.
g) governance by friction, sanction and asymmetric reversibility;

Whenever access, permanence, visibility or contestation are conditioned by opaque sanctions, selective frictions, excessive costs of reaction or asymmetric mechanisms of reversal, there will be an indication of abusive governance of the bond. The corresponding supply duty is to ensure minimally intelligible procedures, verifiable reasoning, a reasonable possibility of contestation and non-arbitrary treatment of the user in the administration of enjoyment. The minimum required evidence falls on sanction records, contestation flow, criteria mobilized, structural difficulties of reversal and concrete impacts of the measure on the continuity of the experience. The possible legal qualification may involve an abusive practice, a safety defect of the service when the legal and procedural security of enjoyment is compromised, in addition to integration into a broader hypothesis of unlawful act of architecture. The institutional consequence includes reversal or review of sanctions, procedural duties, creation or improvement of contestation mechanisms and, in structurally repetitive cases, correction of the ecosystem's enforcement regime.
h) abusive teleology and unlawful act of architecture;

Whenever microfrictions, normalized losses, fabricated urgencies, artificial scarcities, strategic opacity, elastic equivalences and other mechanisms operate in a coordinated way to extract value from vulnerability or to degrade enjoyment as a routine of the environment, there will be a hypothesis of abusive teleology. The corresponding supply duty is not to structure the experience on the basis of an exploitative purpose incompatible with good faith, transparency, balance and protection of the enjoyment legitimately incorporated into the bond. The minimum required evidence consists in the demonstration of the pattern, of its replicability, of the coordination between mechanisms of the ecosystem and of the relevant impact produced on practical autonomy, <1>p. 747</1> intelligibility or utility of the experience. The possible legal qualification reaches structural abusive practice, a defect of the supply regime, possible cumulation with a quality defect and grounds for injunctive and corrective relief over architecture. The institutional consequence goes beyond the reparation of isolated episodes and may include reconfiguration of flows, reinforced transparency duties, design correction and structural or collective measures.
i) evidence in an environment of structural asymmetry;

Whenever the platform concentrates the essential elements for narrating, demonstrating and reconstructing the conflict, the evidentiary discipline must recognize that verifiability is part of the very legitimate regime of supply. The corresponding duty is to preserve and disclose the minimum records necessary for reconstructing the disputed event. The minimum required evidence, from the consumer's point of view, consists in a plausible presentation of the harmful experience, of its insertion in the ecosystem and of the accessible context elements; from the supplier's point of view, disclosure of trails, logs, histories, versions and technically delimited justifications is required. The possible legal qualification involves dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforcement of the duty of cooperation, without prejudice to the material incidence of the other parameters. The institutional consequence consists in preventing technical opacity from becoming procedural shielding and in making effective standards such as open auditability and functional equivalence.
j) reconciliation with intellectual property;

Whenever the platform invokes exclusive ownership, trade secret, licensing or the proprietary structure of the ecosystem to resist control over the mode of supply, reconciliation must be carried out in light of the social function and of the constitutional limits on the exercise of private positions. The corresponding duty is to exercise exclusivity without turning it into a shield for absolute opacity, degrading mutability or arbitrary suppression of enjoyment. The minimum required evidence falls on the relation between the prerogative invoked and the concrete aspect of the conflict, demonstrating whether the restriction is really necessary to protect the asset or whether it operates, in truth, as undue immunization of governance. The possible legal qualification preserves the validity of intellectual property on its own plane, but rules out its invocation as a general veto on the incidence of the CDC. The <1>p. 748</1> institutional consequence consists in reconciling exclusivity and consumer-law protection by means of delimited auditability, control of functional equivalence and subjection of the exercise of IP to the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration.
k) remedies adequate to functional restoration and regime correction.

Whenever the injury affects access, continuity, equivalence, history, relational position or meaningful density of enjoyment, the legal response must prioritize functional restoration, reserving monetary compensation for cases where restoration is unfeasible or insufficient. The corresponding duty is to structure protection in accordance with the nature of the loss, targeting the affected enjoyment and not merely its residual monetary translation. The minimum required evidence involves demonstration of the causal link between the governance mechanism and the functional loss, as well as of the technical or institutional possibility of restoration, reversal, equivalent substitution or procedural correction. The possible legal qualification varies according to the principal incidence of the case, but the institutional consequence must favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent functional substitution, governance adjustments, injunctive relief and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern. Monetization remains possible, but as a residual or complementary response, not as an automatic reflex of the injury.

This framework does not seek to mechanize the decision nor to reduce the complexity of the environment to a rigid formula. Its function is more honest and more useful. It organizes, in consultable language, the passage between governance structure, violated duty, minimum evidentiary requirement, legal qualification and possible institutional consequence. With this, the IOC ceases to be merely a dense conceptual construction and presents itself as a framing technology capable of making manageable, without undue flattening, the relation between governed ecosystem and legal response. It is at this point that the category acquires effective decisional utility.

The legal control of Immaterial Objects of Consumption requires a methodological and dogmatic shift that has not always been carried out with the necessary clarity. In platform-governed ecosystems, the analysis cannot remain centered on isolated clauses, terminal acts detached from context or one-off events artificially separated from the environment that produced them. The center of gravity of the examination must be the regime of <1>p. 749</1> supply, that is, the operating program of the ecosystem, the mechanisms by which enjoyment is administered and the legitimacy filters that make this program institutionally controllable. The shift is necessary because, in relations of this nature, what the consumer faces is not merely an episodic manifestation of private power, but a continuous arrangement for organizing experience, access, intelligibility, visibility, contestation and evidence.

The first guideline, therefore, consists in treating architecture and governance not as a neutral backdrop of the bond, but as constitutive elements of supply itself. The environment does not merely host the consumer relationship. It materially shapes it. It is through architecture that the platform defines paths, intensifies or attenuates frictions, selects saliences, organizes degrees of reversibility, distributes costs of understanding and establishes the conditions under which loss will be perceived, expectation will be frustrated and reaction will be possible or unfeasible. It is through governance that the supplier administers permanence, sanction, updating, priority, visibility and mechanisms of contestation. When this structure is rendered legally invisible, control is impoverished. One comes to discuss only final acts detached from an ecosystem whose design, in practice, has already predetermined much of the disputed experience.

From this follows a second guideline. Relevant changes to the service, rule changes, ordinary reconfigurations of the environment and modulations with material impact on enjoyment should not be judged on the basis of a generic discourse of updating, innovation or technical convenience. They must be examined in light of open auditability and functional value equivalence. The relevant question is not only whether the platform could make the change. The question is whether the change was made institutionally intelligible and whether it preserved, in substantial terms, the function that justified the acquisition and structured the consumer's legitimate expectation. The mere appeal to the dynamism of the digital cannot work as an abstract authorization to degrade the experience, obscure the modulation of the environment or turn mutability into an ordinary technology of loss.

The third guideline bears on private sanctions with material impact. In platform ecosystems, sanctions do not operate merely as a one-off disciplinary response to conduct attributed to the user. They may affect access, permanence, visibility, reputation, relational insertion and continuity of enjoyment. For this reason, they must be controlled by denser criteria than the mere formal existence of sanctioning power. They require verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation. Where the platform exercises power of inclusion, exclusion, suspension, visibility downgrading or functional restriction, it is not enough <1>p. 750</1> that the final act be formally communicable. The procedure must be institutionally reconstructible and contestation must not be a mere empty ritual. The examination, in such cases, must reach not only the challenged act, but the procedural conditions designed by the supplier itself for adhesion, enjoyment, evidence and resistance.

This requirement leads to the fourth guideline. The dispute should not be read only from the terminal moment at which it becomes outwardly manifest. It must be reconstructed from the environment in which it arose, was perceived and can be reconstituted. This means that judges and protection bodies need to consider the way in which the platform organized, from the outset, the conditions of adhesion, understanding, circulation of information, access to records and possibility of contestation. The litigious experience, in continuous digital services, already reaches the proceedings traversed by private filters of perception and evidence. Ignoring this fact means accepting that the supplier controls not only enjoyment, but also the way in which the conflict will be narrated institutionally. The case, therefore, needs to be seen in its trajectory and not only in its outcome.

The fifth guideline concerns structural opacity. It should not be treated as an inevitable and legally neutral characteristic of digital complexity. It must be recognized as a factor that intensifies vulnerability and evidentiary asymmetry. Where the platform concentrates logs, histories, change records, interface trails, curation criteria and decision data, there is a correlated concentration of power over the institutional conditions of evidence. This fact justifies orders for preservation and disclosure of minimum records, delimitation of expert examinations and dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof whenever the relevant evidence arises and remains under the supplier's technical control. Opacity, in other words, cannot operate as a procedural privilege self-generated by the governance model itself.

A sixth guideline consists in avoiding both the fragmentation of the problem into individual lawsuits incapable of reaching the source of the injury and the opposite temptation of turning each case into a manifesto against technology or against the economic model as such. Control must be specific enough to respond to the concrete conflict and attentive enough to structure to identify when this conflict is a localized manifestation of a repeated pattern. Neither atomization nor grandiloquence. The institutional challenge lies in recognizing when the case reveals an individual inadequacy correctable without further expansion and when, on the contrary, it exposes a regime defect, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary mode of operation of the ecosystem. This distinction is essential to calibrate the legal response and to prevent programmatic harms from being treated as a mere sum of private annoyances disconnected from one another.

<1>p. 751</1> Hence the seventh guideline, concerning remedies. In cases of architectural injury, the legal response must favor functional restoration and procedural correction, instead of automatically resorting to monetization. When what has been affected is the continuity of enjoyment, the integrity of the experience, the permanence of access, the intelligibility of the bond or the consumer's relational position in the ecosystem, a mere monetary award tends to operate as a poor and structurally ineffective remedy. What is required, whenever possible, is restoration of access, reversal or review of sanctions, restoration of functionality, preservation of history, equivalent substitution and adjustment of governance procedures. This priority is even clearer when the injury stems not from an isolated episode, but from the very design of the supply regime and its ordinary mode of operation.

The eighth guideline emerges precisely from this point. When the pattern of injury proves to be repeated, replicable and incorporated into the structure of the environment, protection should not be limited to the single case. Room opens for injunctive relief and for regime correction measures. This includes procedural duties, architecture adjustments, reinforced auditability requirements, review of sanction flows, imposition of intelligible contestation channels and other measures capable of reaching the continuous source of the problem. The system cannot treat programmatic harms as a casual accumulation of autonomous conflicts. When the injury is programmatic, the response must also be structurally sensitive to the program that produces it.

A ninth guideline consists in preserving institutional sobriety. Control of architecture and governance does not require the judge to become the system's engineer nor the protection body to hold full technical mastery of the ecosystem. What is required is something at once more modest and more serious: the capacity to bring the environment back to verifiable filters of legitimacy. Open auditability, functional equivalence, verifiable reasoning, procedural coherence, minimum intelligibility of contestation, preservation of essential records and functional reconciliation between exclusivity and consumer-law protection are sufficient criteria to make the conflict decidable without any pretension to technical omniscience. The complexity of the digital does not eliminate Law. It only requires Law to choose more rigorously what it needs to understand in order to control.

Finally, a tenth guideline requires that institutional examination preserve unity among supply, evidence and remedy. In IOCs, these planes cannot be rigidly compartmentalized. The way the object is offered interferes with the way the loss will be perceived. The way enjoyment is governed conditions the way the conflict can be proven. The way architecture distributes access and opacity influences the adequacy of the remedy. Artificially separating these planes produces decisions that are formally organized but <1>p. 752</1> materially blind. Effective control depends on seeing them as parts of one and the same legal problem. That is what makes it possible to treat architecture and governance as elements of supply and not as a technically interesting but legally irrelevant backdrop.

These guidelines, taken together, offer an application criterion that rejects both atomized examination and inflamed generalization. What is proposed is more useful. A way of reading continuous digital conflicts from the regime that produces them, subjecting architecture and governance to the legitimacy filters that make private power institutionally controllable. It is at this point that the IOC ceases to be merely a descriptive category of new environments and asserts itself as a decision instrument able to organize evidence, qualification and legal response without the technical complexity of the environment operating as a practical obstacle to control.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption reveals, in the end, an institutional fact that cannot be treated as peripheral. In platform ecosystems, supply no longer falls only on economically appreciable utilities in the narrow sense. It increasingly bears on practical conditions of participation, visibility, reputation, permanence and contestation in environments that structure relevant portions of contemporary social life. This does not mean dissolving the consumer relationship into an abstract political category, nor replacing dogmatic analysis with grandiose sociological rhetoric. It means recognizing that, in long-lasting immaterial objects of consumption, governed enjoyment may be part of processes of biographical continuity, relational insertion and symbolic identity, so that unilateral sanctions, erasures, reconfigurations and degradations may reach dimensions of the experience that exceed the residual patrimonial.

This point is especially important because it prevents an impoverished reading of the conflict. When enjoyment is long, cumulative and socially situated, the object consumed ceases to be merely a utility detachable from the user's trajectory. It may become an anchoring point of history, belonging, reputation, memory of use and recognition before third parties. In these cases, functional loss is not limited to a momentary unavailability of access nor to a one-off economic frustration. It may compromise continuity of presence, stability of bonds, intelligibility of the consumer's own trajectory in the environment and preservation of symbolic elements that, although economically mediated, take on practical existential <1>p. 753</1> relevance. This is not a matter of inflating any digital discomfort to the condition of an identity drama. It is a matter of recognizing that certain environments of governed enjoyment operate on concrete dimensions of personal integrity in a functional sense.

The formulation of these limits, however, requires conceptual sobriety. This is not a matter of equating platform with State, nor of converting the CDC into a parallel constitution of digital life. This comparison, besides being crude, tends to produce more smoke than light. The premise is another, and far more defensible. Functional public relevance does not produce equivalence to the State, but neither does it authorize treating the platform as an institutionally neutral supplier. When private powers administer access, permanence, visibility, reputation and contestation in environments structurally relevant to social participation, the legal order already has legal matrices of limitation. The Constitution is one of them. The CDC is another, operating in reconciliation with the social function of property, with the discipline of intellectual property and with the general limits on the exercise of private positions in a constitutionally oriented economic order.

Under this key, the CDC appears with greater density than that of a mere microsystem devoted to the discipline of one-off patrimonial exchanges. In environments of governed participation, it also functions as one of the legal matrices for limiting private power, precisely because the supply regime comes to organize concrete conditions of presence, interaction, permanence and contestation. This does not alter its nature nor transform it into an instrument of total publicization of the consumer relationship. It only makes explicit its aptitude to control, in a constitutionally compatible key, forms of supply that are no longer exhausted in the simple circulation of goods or in the episodic provision of services, but structure relevant portions of the consumer's social experience.

This conclusion matters because it puts the category of the IOC back in its proper institutional reach. Control of the immaterial object of consumption is neither a cultural gesture nor a theoretical whim, nor is it reduced to an attempt to update the CDC terminologically. It is a dogmatically necessary response to environments that tend to produce opacity, mutability and private concentration of power as normal operating conditions. In them, the precariousness of enjoyment cannot be naturalized by the mere invocation of contract, license, innovation or the global scale of the service. The function of the regime is to reintroduce institutional controllability where the supplier seeks to pass off contingency as the user's inevitable destiny.

This reintroduction of controllability is particularly relevant when the supplier presents itself as a mere intermediary, as neutral technology or as a global provider whose private normativity would purport to replace, by self-reference, the local legal vocabulary. <1>p. 754</1> In each of these figures there is a recurring attempt to shift the discussion outside the field of attribution. The intermediary will say that it merely connects. Neutral technology will say that it merely executes. The global provider will say that it merely operates according to its own universal terms. The IOC regime rejects these self-descriptions as a sufficient framing criterion. What matters is not how the platform names itself, but how it organizes access, permanence, visibility, contestation and enjoyment. Whenever this organization produces legal relevance under the discipline of supply, there will be room for the incidence of limits, duties and consequences.

This is also why the digital citizenship implied here should not be read as a loose, celebratory category or one disconnected from dogmatics. It appears as a functional problem of participation under private governance. The point is not to assert rights in the abstract before an idealized public sphere, but to recognize that, in certain ecosystems, the consumption experience directly touches the practical conditions of presence and agency of the individual. Digital citizenship, in this context, does not replace the IOC regime. It helps to illuminate why certain conflicts of governed enjoyment cannot be treated as mere low-density contractual annoyances. When the platform administers the entry doors, the criteria of permanence, the mechanisms of visibility and the means of contestation, it comes to affect dimensions of practical autonomy that Law cannot abandon to pure corporate self-legitimation.

The strategic consequence of this for typological application is clear. From this point on, the incidence of the IOC regime becomes recognizable in different families of platform without depending on the cultural sensitivity of the reader or the judge to perceive, intuitively, the seriousness of the environment. The argument no longer needs emotional adherence to the social importance of a given service and comes to operate through criteria of supply, governance and limitation of private power. This strengthens the transposability of the regime. Even when the platform presents itself under discourses of neutrality, innovation, globality or mere intermediation, the analysis can bring the case back to what really matters: who organizes enjoyment, who administers its intelligibility, who controls its permanence and who defines the conditions of its contestation.

The legal dispute in governed ecosystems is already born traversed by regimes of perception administered by the supplier itself. The consumer does not enter the conflict on neutral ground. They enter an environment whose language, memory, visibility and possibilities of reaction were previously designed by the party that also concentrates economic, technical and normative power over the relationship. The dogmatic response, therefore, needs to recover agency, <1>p. 755</1> verifiability and controllability. Not to freeze the service, nor to deny the complexity of the environment, but to prevent precariousness, opacity and asymmetric mutability from being accepted as the natural state of things. Because when private power begins to govern participation as if it were weather, and not an institutionally controllable choice, Law is already far too late.

The passage from the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to its incidence in different families of platform requires an operative grid capable of preserving dogmatic unity in distinct contexts. When continuous immaterial consumption is organized by private architectures of access, visibility, permanence, curation and ordinary mutation, the conflict cannot be resolved by the appearance of the sector nor by the degree of social familiarity with the technology involved. It is necessary to bring the case back to parameters dense enough to stabilize institutional expectations, guide the formation of evidence and allow consistent normative consequences.

This requirement stems from the very nature of the bond. In platform-governed ecosystems, enjoyment is not exhausted in a one-off act of delivery, nor can it be understood as a neutral reality on which only lateral contractual clauses bear. What is offered to the consumer is an experience legally shaped by continuous mechanisms of private organization, whose effects fall on access, intelligibility, equivalence, permanence and contestation. For this reason, the controllability of the regime does not depend on inventorying technologies or classifying markets, but on establishing criteria that make legible the power structure that modulates enjoyment. Without this mediation, application degrades into descriptive casuistry or impressionistic judgment, oscillating between uncritical fascination and generic aversion to technique.

The parameters synthesized at the end of the preceding dogmatic reconstruction then take on a properly operative function. They no longer present themselves as mere moments of theoretical <1>p. 715</1> elaboration, but as references applicable to the institutional reading of the conflict. Their usefulness lies in reducing dependence on the interpreter's subjective repertoires and in containing the tendency, recurrent in digital litigation, to decide on the basis of vague impressions about innovation, technical complexity or business freedom. The digital condition, by itself, decides nothing. Nor does the sectoral label of the service. What decides, legally, is the way in which the environment organizes private power, redistributes capacities of understanding and contestation and produces relevant frictions on the consumption experience.

The application of these parameters is guided by a repeatable sequence. One starts from the predominant governance mechanism and the type of friction it produces. The central vulnerability triggered in the bond is identified. The standard of evidence compatible with the structure of the conflict is established. Finally, the possible dogmatic consequence under the IOC regime is indicated.

The sequence works as a controllability lock. Its function is to prevent both the decomposition of the conflict into isolated clauses, one-off events or contingent failures, as if the relationship could be understood from fragments detached from a structurally governed experience, and the replacement of legal analysis by a diffuse impression about technology, innovation or technical complexity, in which the interpreter oscillates between excessive deference and generic distrust without managing to convert the environment examined into normatively tractable facts. Both distortions result from the same error of perspective. They ignore that, in continuous digital services, enjoyment is not an external consequence of the contract, but a permanent space of private shaping of the experience.

The first task, therefore, consists in recognizing the presence of an immaterial object of consumption subject to continuous, reconfigurable or modulable provision. This recognition does not stem from the name of the service, the social image of the sector or the mere presence of a digital interface. It stems from the legally relevant way in which access, permanence, intelligibility, equivalence and contestation are organized throughout enjoyment. Once this regime is identified, it becomes possible to qualify semiotic vulnerability not as a subjective attribute of the user nor as an imprecise environmental label, but as a mechanism of power bearing on the bond. It is this qualification that makes it possible to reorganize duties and unlawful acts around informational adequacy, advertising, legibility and governance standards of the environment, without reducing the question to individual cognitive insufficiency or to a moral defect of technology.

On this basis, the legitimacy filters built on the dogmatic plane come into operation, with centrality for open auditability, functional value equivalence and <1>p. 716</1> abusive teleology. These filters make it possible to distinguish legitimate modulations of provision from changes that structurally degrade enjoyment, obscure the intelligibility of the bond or incorporate an exploitative orientation incompatible with the limits of the CDC and with the constitutional containment of private power by architecture. Their relevance lies in providing verifiable attribution criteria, capable of organizing decisional reasoning without requiring exhaustive technical mastery of the ecosystem by the judge. This is not a matter of freezing innovation, nor of requiring absolute transparency about all of the supplier's internal processes. It is a matter of imposing sufficient parameters of institutional translation so that governance, mutability and friction can be brought back to discernible duties, unlawful acts, evidentiary burdens and remedies.

The requirement, consequently, is not the exhaustive observation of all contemporary digital markets, but the demonstration that the regime retains a capacity for controllable incidence when confronted with diverse arrangements of continuous supply by platform. What one seeks to verify is whether these parameters manage to produce legal qualification, organize evidence and guide normative consequence in distinct environments, without losing precision and without depending on intuitive impressions about the sector examined. Therein lies their relevance and also their pertinence. They do not have the power to replace the complexity of the real, but they prevent this complexity from being used as an alibi for irresponsibility over architecture.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption on services of cognitive functionality is not defined by the label of “artificial intelligence”, “assistant”, “chat” or “productivity tool”, but by the governance structure that modulates, over time, the utility delivered and the possibility of reconstructing promise, change and functional impact through accessible evidence.

In this family, provision is not exhausted in the one-off issuing of a response, in the isolated display of content or in the supply of a singly considered piece of data. What is offered is an environment of cognitive orientation. It is a functional infrastructure that organizes how the user understands the problem submitted, trusts the response received, incorporates it into their decision-making, reviews it, corrects it or reassesses it in the face of error, oscillation or change in performance. The legally relevant core of the subtype therefore lies in the informational integrity of the enjoyment regime, in the epistemic trust that sustains the functional use of the service and in the institutional possibility of reconstructing the link between promise, delivery, change and impact.

This configuration rules out, from the outset, two inadequate reductions. The first is to treat the conflict as a mere discussion about an isolated factual error, as if the utility of the service came down to the abstract correctness of each individual response. The second is to reduce the analysis to the generic contractual vocabulary of software licensing or of the technical provision of informational support. Neither reading reaches the central problem.

<1>p. 758</1> In services of this nature, the utility consumed consists precisely in offering practical orientation in conversational, synthetic, contextual or responsive form, so that the user's experience comes to depend on an environment whose real intelligibility, operational limits and patterns of change are not mastered by them. What is at stake is not only the content issued, but the regime of functional trust in which this content is received, used and converted into conduct.

Enjoyment, here, must be read as governed cognitive enjoyment. The user does not consume only information in raw form. They consume a private arrangement of selection, formulation, prioritization, synthesis, interface language and presentation of responses that organizes the very experience of useful knowledge. This governance is especially sensitive because it operates on an object whose utility depends on practical trust. The service is valuable not only because it responds, but because it induces the user to treat the response as a relevant point of orientation.

Whenever this environment is structurally opaque as to the operating criteria that condition error, instability, change in performance, contextual limitation or later reconstruction of the interaction, a typical field of incidence of the IOC is established. The central vulnerability, here, is not mere technical ignorance on the part of the user. It is semiotic vulnerability intensified by epistemic dependence, that is, by subjection to an environment that administers the signs of reliability, utility and sufficiency of the response without granting, to the same extent, means of verification and audit to the recipient.

A reading of the official terms reinforces precisely this nature of governed service. OpenAI's Terms of Use state that they apply to the use of ChatGPT and of the company's other services for individuals, together with associated applications, software and websites, and subordinate this use to compliance with complementary policies, documentation and guidelines, which evidences continuous provision organized by private rules of operation and modulation of the environment <1>OPENAI</1><2>(OpenAI, 2026)</2>.

In the case of Gemini, Google's own official page of services and specific terms indicates that the Gemini Apps are subject to Google's general Terms of Service and to the Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy, which likewise reveals an environment of continuous supply governed by its own normative layer, and not a simple instantaneous delivery of neutral content <1>GOOGLE</1><2>(Google, [202-?])</2>. In both cases, the contractual frame does not describe mere access to a static tool. It describes entry into an ecosystem of regulated use, subject to conditioning, limitation and reorganization by private governance.

This fact is dogmatically important because it allows the subtype to be brought back to the IOC regime without depending on fragile analogies. The cognitive utility supplied does not present itself <1>p. 759</1> as an autonomous thing, fully inspectable outside the environment. It depends on the continuity of the system, the relative stability of the interface, the maintenance of the conditions of access, the model of presentation of the responses, the warnings, the contextual limits, the mechanisms of memory or history where they exist, and the private rules that structure the very field of use. In other words, enjoyment resides not only in the individual response, but in the functional arrangement that makes it possible to trust, use, review and contest the provision. In this key, the legal problem ceases to be the abstract quality of the information and becomes the controllability of the informational regime as a form of supply.

Relevant inadequacy may take, in this subtype, forms of its own. There may be informational noise when the architecture of the response projects an appearance of security, completeness or sufficiency incompatible with the real limits of the provision. There may be functional opacity when the user cannot reconstruct, in minimally verifiable terms, why a given output was presented to them, to what extent there was a relevant change in the system's behavior or which elements of the environment conditioned the response that guided their conduct. There may also be acute evidentiary asymmetry when the functional impact of the provision depends on history, interactional context, internal parameters or records that remain concentrated in the supplier. In these scenarios, the injury need not appear as a direct lie to be legally relevant. It is enough that the environment replaces legibility with a performance of trust, shifting onto the user the cost of bearing error, review, oscillation or functional loss without adequate institutional trails of reconstruction.

The consequence is that, in this family, open auditability takes on an even more central role than in other subtypes. This is not a matter of requiring unrestricted opening of the model, code or internal architecture. It is a matter of recognizing that, in services whose utility consists in cognitively guiding the user, there must be minimum institutional verifiability over relevant aspects of the provision. This includes, as the case may be, preservation of accessible history, minimum traces of interaction, sufficient explanation of materially relevant limits, intelligibility about changes in the regime of use and the possibility of reconstructing the link between the functional promise of the service and the impact produced on the user's experience. Without this, the platform retains not only the power to provide guidance, but also the power to define unilaterally what can be narrated and proven when this guidance proves inadequate, inconsistent or harmful.

The standard of evidence compatible with this subtype cannot, for this reason, naively reproduce the logic of the isolated event. The relevant evidence tends to require reconstruction of the informational journey, of the context of use, of the available interactional history, of the <1>p. 760</1> warnings present or absent, of the form of presentation of the response and of the practical function it performed in the user's decision. It also tends to require caution regarding recurrent blind spots. The first is the tendency to reduce the conflict to the sentence issued, ignoring the semiotic architecture that made it reliable or operational. The second is the tendency to presume that generic warnings about the system's limitations would suffice, by themselves, to neutralize any problem of informational adequacy. The third is the tendency to treat the model's variability as a raw fact of technique, and not as a governed element whose opacity needs to be legally bearable.

The possible dogmatic consequence, in this type of environment, usually gravitates around an informational quality defect of supply, an abusive practice by functional opacity, insufficiency of the duty to inform and reinforcement of verifiability duties compatible with the cognitive enjoyment promised. In more serious cases, especially when the architecture of the service repeatedly administers practical trust without proportional instruments of reconstruction and contestation, there may be room for a reading in the key of abusive teleology, particularly if opacity is not a mere technical residue but a stable part of the mode of exploitation of the environment. The most adequate institutional response will tend to favor procedural correction, reinforcement of verifiable trails, review of the communicational arrangement and functional restoration of the injured trust, instead of mere abstract monetization of the conflict.

The subtype thus shows clearly the expansive usefulness of the IOC regime. Even outside the original laboratory in which the thesis was densified, a structure of supply remains recognizable in which utility, trust, opacity and evidence are administered by the supplier in continuous and governed form. What changes is the matter on which this governance bears. Here, it falls on cognitive orientation and on the very functional intelligibility of the provision. Precisely for this reason, enjoyment cannot be treated as a simple reception of content, but as a governed informational experience, dependent on private operating criteria that need to be brought back to auditability, adequacy and institutional controllability.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption on infrastructure and intermediation platforms is not defined by the final object traded nor by the traditional economic classification of the sector in which the platform operates. Its point of support lies in the governance structure that organizes the very possibility of exchange, encounter, circulation and <1>p. 761</1> comparison in a digitally administered environment. In this family, the utility supplied is not exhausted in the presence of a good, a piece of content, an advertiser or a user finalizable at one end of the relationship. What is offered, in legally relevant terms, is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics without which the final object does not become economically legible, socially rankable or practically accessible in the terms in which the platform itself presents it.

This fact requires dogmatic care because the recurrent self-description of these platforms tends to reduce them to the function of merely bringing parties together. In their formal language, they frequently appear as neutral spaces of encounter between seller and buyer, between sender and receiver, between advertiser and audience, between content producers and the public. This description, although partially true on a superficial plane, is insufficient to capture the real structure of supply. Platforms of this nature do not merely connect. They select, rank, highlight, hide, bring closer, delay, prioritize and reorganize the way in which the reality of the environment becomes perceptible to the user. The market, the offer and even the social relevance of what circulates within it appear to the consumer and to the user through private filters of visibility, salience and intelligibility.

This family of platforms must be treated as that of suppliers of semantic infrastructures of the exchange environments themselves, since their users do not consume only products sold by third parties, posts displayed in a <1>feed</1> or content that appears before their screen. They consume, before that, private frames that define what will be seen as most relevant, most reliable, most comparable, safest, most popular or most worthy of attention. Enjoyment, in this case, is strongly governed by interface. <2>Rankings</2>, reputation, highlighting, recommendation, prioritization and modulation of reach are not peripheral elements. They are part of the functional utility of the ecosystem and directly influence the formation of expectation, the assessment of risk and the possibility of rational choice.

In <1>marketplaces</1>, this logic manifests itself with special clarity. Mercado Livre's Terms and Conditions of Use describe an ecosystem in which the platform organizes not only the publication of listings, but also rules of use, visibility, intermediation, payments, reputation, logistics and dispute resolution, inserting the buying and selling experience into an environment densely governed by private infrastructure <2>MERCADO LIVRE</2><3>(Mercado Livre, 2026)</3>. The same is seen in Magalu's Purchase and Sale Terms, in which the platform regulates the conditions of marketing in the marketplace, including distinguishing its own offers from those of partners, but reserving for itself the organization of the environment in which such offers will be <4>p. 762</4> perceived, compared and consumed <5>MAGAZINE LUIZA</5><6>(Magazine Luiza, [202-?])</6>. In both cases, the platform does not limit itself to hosting listings. It administers criteria of presentation, trust, prioritization and legibility of the market accessible to the consumer.

The dogmatic consequence is relevant. The consumer does not choose in a vacuum, before a transparent and symmetrical universe of offers. They choose within a field already pre-interpreted by the platform. The prominent position of an item, the appearance of reliability of a seller, the way reviews are displayed, the distinction between sponsored and organically prioritized products, the integration with means of payment and logistics, the organization of categories and the form of display of alternatives are all elements that materially interfere with the consumption experience. The platform, therefore, produces the perceptible market itself. It transforms a chaotic multiplicity of offers into an administered semantic environment, in which comparability between alternatives already reaches the consumer filtered by criteria they do not control and often cannot even reconstruct in a verifiable way.

This mechanism is not limited to e-commerce in the strict sense. On social networks, the same functional structure reappears in a different form. Meta's Terms of Service describe an environment in which the use of Facebook is subject to private rules of permanence, visibility, sharing, moderation and organization of the circulating content, so that the user's experience is mediated by internal criteria of distribution and management of social interaction <1>FACEBOOK</1><2>(Facebook, [202-?])</2>. X's Rules and policies, in turn, show a platform equally oriented by private discipline of circulation, authenticity, safety and standards of participation, which evidences that visibility, permanence and reputation do not appear as neutral data, but as results of concentrated governance <3>X CORP</3><4>(X Corp, [202-?])</4>. Here too, the platform does not merely “let appear” content produced by third parties. It administers the way in which this content enters the user's field of perception and how its relevance is socially stabilized.

This rapprochement between marketplaces and social networks does not seek to erase evident sectoral differences between buying and selling, on the one hand, and the social circulation of content, on the other. What matters, for the typology developed here, is the functional equivalence of the predominant mechanism. In both cases, the platform governs the environment of appearance. In both, it administers salience, reputation, comparability and intelligibility. In both, the user depends on a private interface that pre-organizes the space in which the decision will occur, whether that decision is a purchase, a choice between sellers, a reputational adherence, a click, an interaction or the very formation of judgment about what is socially relevant. The utility supplied, therefore, is not reduced to the final object circulating in the environment. It includes the very <1>p. 763</1> architecture that transforms circulation into ordered experience and that converts an abundance of possibilities into a governed field of perception and choice.

It is precisely there that the central vulnerability of this subtype emerges. It is semiotic vulnerability intensified by structural dependence on the interface as producer of the accessible real. The user faces not only information asymmetry in a quantitative sense. They face asymmetry in the constitution of the relevant field of decision. The platform defines what stands out, what is hidden, what seems most reliable, what acquires the appearance of consensus, what appears as comparable and what becomes practically invisible. In such environments, the supplier's promise lies not only in the explicit discourse of neutrality, efficiency or convenience. It lies also in the implicit promise of intelligibility of the market or of social circulation. When this intelligibility is governed by opaque criteria, non-transparent internal interests or non-auditable ranking standards, enjoyment comes to be affected in its very core of legibility.

The evidence compatible with this type of conflict requires a more careful institutional reconstruction than that normally mobilized in classic litigation over an isolated offer. It is not enough to examine the final product acquired or the individual content removed, prioritized or hidden. It is necessary to reconstruct the architecture of the experience. This includes, as the case may be, the form of presentation of offers, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of reviews and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the reliability signals provided by the interface, the context of appearance of the content, the relevant moderation criteria and the mechanisms by which the platform induces a perception of market, consensus or priority. On social networks, this reconstruction may further involve examining the way in which the feed, recommendation, reach and reputational management condition the very perception of what is in circulation. In marketplaces, it may involve the way in which <1>ranking</1>, highlighting, seller classification and sponsorship logic produce a perceptible market already preselected.

There are, in this subtype, recurrent blind spots that need to be avoided. The first is the tendency to treat the interface as a mere visual support, and not as a constitutive part of supply. The second is the tendency to imagine that the platform would answer legally only for what it said expressly in a clause or in advertising, as if the effective governance of visibility were legally irrelevant. The third is the tendency to reduce the dispute to the terminal act, such as the frustrated purchase, the removal of a piece of content or the supposed preference for a given offer, without investigating the private structure of salience that conditioned the user's entire experience. These blind spots are especially dangerous <1>p. 764</1> because they allow the platform to preserve, under an appearance of technical neutrality, decisive power over the material conditions of choice and appearance.

The possible dogmatic consequence, in this environment, tends to gravitate around procedural duties of controllability of interface governance. When the platform organizes the very perceptible field of exchange or social circulation, it is not enough to discuss only liability for the final object or for the isolated conduct of a third party. It becomes necessary to examine, in the key of the IOC, whether there was adequate information about the nature of the intermediation, whether the distinction between organic priority and sponsored priority was materially intelligible, whether the reputation displayed was functionally verifiable, whether the opacity of the criteria compromised relevant comparability and whether the interface itself produced deceptiveness, obscuring or structural asymmetry incompatible with the consumer-law regime. In more serious cases, especially when the platform acts simultaneously as arbiter of the environment and as an economic agent interested in its results, the opacity of ranking may also connect with broader abusive practices and with competition repercussions of their own.

In this family, open auditability and functional equivalence operate as transversal filters. Open auditability requires minimum institutional verifiability over the relevant criteria of presentation, prioritization, moderation, reputation and circulation, without this implying unrestricted opening of internal systems. What is demanded is sufficient intelligibility to understand how the environment organizes the user's experience and how certain choices of the platform interfere with the formation of expectation, with comparability between alternatives and with the possibility of contestation. Functional equivalence, in turn, applies when changes to the intermediation regime, to the logic of visibility, to reputational criteria or to the rules of circulation relevantly degrade the utility legitimately incorporated into the bond, without compatible restoration. This may occur both in e-commerce and in the social circulation of content, whenever the platform substantially alters the functional role of the infrastructure it offered as an environment of exchange, reach or recognition.

The subtype thus demonstrates that the infrastructure and intermediation platform is not a mere neutral corridor through which previously formed wills circulate. It is an agent in the construction of the field in which these wills become possible, perceptible and operationalizable. That is why the IOC regime applies with particular force in this environment. What is controlled is not only the correctness of the final object traded or of the content terminally presented. What is controlled is the semiotic governance of the very space of <1>p. 765</1> circulation, that is, the way in which the supplier administers relevance, trust, comparability and appearance. When this administration takes place under structural opacity, non-verifiable criteria or implicit promises of neutrality incompatible with the practice of the ecosystem, consumer-law incidence ceases to be a rhetorical expansion and becomes a simple requirement of institutional controllability of supply.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption on work platforms under the gig economy requires starting from a structural fact. In this family, the central utility is not reduced to the final payment per ride, delivery or completed task. What is supplied, in functional terms, is a private infrastructure of economic possibility. The platform organizes access to demand, distribution of calls, minimum predictability of remuneration, permanence in the productive flow, reputational criteria, prioritization standards, acceptance rules and sanction mechanisms. The object enjoyed, here, is not a static good nor a simple service externally provided to the worker. It is a governed productive environment, without which everyday economic activity does not become viable in the terms in which the platform itself promised and structured it.

This point is important because it prevents the analysis from being captured by excessively formal narratives about contractual autonomy. The instruments used by iFood, 99Food, Uber and 99 insist, with variations of language, on characterizing partners as independent, on presenting the platform as an environment of technological intermediation and on ruling out a hierarchical bond or mandatory exclusivity. iFood's terms for couriers speak of independent activity, of freedom as to when, how and where to make deliveries and of the company's role as a connection between customers, establishments and couriers <1>IFOOD</1><2>(iFood, [2023?])</2>. 99's terms for partner drivers and motorcyclists follow the same line, presenting 99 as the intermediary of a marketplace, describing the partner as an autonomous and independent professional and providing for the platform's remuneration for the intermediation, as well as acceptance and completion metrics and temporary ride restrictions <3>99</3><4>(99, [202-?])</4>. Uber's General Terms of Use, in turn, also cover the making of deliveries by an independent partner at the location indicated in the app, while the Uber Community Guidelines make explicit that their rules apply to users, partner drivers and couriers, which reveals unified governance of permanence and behavior in the ecosystem <5>UBER</5><6>(Uber, 2026)</6>.

<1>p. 766</1> None of this, however, suffices to resolve the dogmatic problem. The legally relevant question is not only whether the platform describes itself as an intermediary or whether the partner is formally free to switch the app on and off. The question is another. It is a matter of recognizing that the functional utility indispensable to the exercise of economic activity is offered, modulated and reconfigured by a private architecture that the subject does not control. The formal freedom to join or leave the environment coexists, here, with intense dependence on the private conditions of access to demand, calculation of earnings, formation of reputation, reading of performance and maintenance of eligibility in the productive flow. Enjoyment, therefore, is productive enjoyment of a governed environment. The platform worker consumes the very infrastructure that makes them economically operative.

It is precisely there that the subtype differs from a generic labor-law reading. The central point lies not only in asserting algorithmic subordination in the abstract, nor in automatically reclassifying the entire relationship under traditional categories of the employment contract. The focus, for the purposes of this typology, is on the supply regime. The platform supplies an ecosystem whose utility consists in making possible the exercise of economic activity under private conditions of visibility, distribution, prioritization and permanence. Income does not arise outside the environment and merely pass through it. It depends materially on the architecture of the environment. Whenever this architecture concentrates access criteria, unilaterally modulates the functional value of permanence and makes opaque the elements needed to understand losses, drops in demand, downgrades or restrictions, there will be a typical field of incidence of the IOC.

In this family, the central vulnerability takes a particularly acute form. It is semiotic vulnerability associated with productive dependence. The partner depends on the platform not only to obtain calls, rides or deliveries. They also depend on the internal signs by which the environment informs their position, projects reliability, organizes expectation of earnings, justifies variations in remuneration and communicates the risk of restriction or exclusion. Metrics, incentive messages, quality alerts, promotions, acceptance standards, pricing dynamics and performance notifications operate as a private language for governing conduct. This is not simple neutral operational information. It is a semiotic regime that organizes the subject's economic experience and redistributes onto them the costs of interpreting an environment whose material functioning they cannot audit autonomously.

This structure appears clearly in the materials examined. iFood states that it does not supervise the courier's activities “through the platform or by any other means”, but at the same time provides for ratings, analysis of complaints, minimum criteria related to the <1>p. 767</1> obligations assumed before customers and establishments and cases of deactivation and inactivation on the platform <2>IFOOD</2><3>(iFood, [2023?])</3>. 99, even more explicitly, structures the governance of the partner through an intermediation fee, objective criteria for use of the app, acceptance and completion metrics, the possibility of temporary ride restriction and account cancellation in cases defined at its sole discretion, including for registration issues and inappropriate conduct <4>99</4><5>(99, [202-?])</5>. The overall design is eloquent. The platform asserts independence at the contractual end and intensifies governance at the operational end.

That is why the dogmatic problem cannot be reduced to the simplistic dichotomy between autonomy and subordination. What is at stake is the legal control of a private productive infrastructure that materially conditions the continuity of the partner's economic life. Opacity about the distribution of opportunities, prioritization criteria, variable remuneration parameters, the effects of ratings and the causality of restrictions falls, in this context, not only on abstract contractual comfort, but on the very material conditions of life of subjects who depend on this environment to work. The governance of the app, here, does not regulate merely a user experience. It regulates access to income, minimum predictability of livelihood and the practical possibility of remaining economically active.

Hence the centrality of open auditability in this subtype. Relevant rule changes, changes in calculation, reconfigurations of priority, redefinitions of metrics or sanctions with material impact cannot be shielded by a generic discourse of efficiency, safety or algorithmic optimization. They must be made minimally verifiable. This does not mean fully opening the system, nor turning the Judiciary into the technical administrator of the platform. It means requiring sufficient institutional intelligibility about what relevantly affects the distribution of opportunities, the formation of earnings, the incidence of restrictions and the functional continuity of the partner's permanence in the ecosystem. Without this minimum, the platform simultaneously concentrates the power to organize economic activity and the power to make opaque the facts needed to contest it.

In environments of captive productive enjoyment, mutability is not limited to updating the interface or improving operation. It can substantially degrade the functional utility of the partner's permanence. Changes in call distribution criteria, pricing parameters, eligibility rules, incentive models or reputational weights may keep the name of the program, the appearance of the partnership and even the formal existence of the account, but relevantly empty the economic utility that justified joining and sustained the continuity of productive enjoyment. The legal test cannot be only whether the account remains <1>p. 768</1> active. It must be whether the partner's functional position in the environment remains substantially equivalent to the one that structured their legitimate expectation of earnings and permanence.

The standard of evidence compatible with this type of conflict requires a more sophisticated reconstruction of the productive experience. It is not enough to show that there was a reduction in earnings or a one-off block. It is necessary to reconstruct the relation between governance mechanism and functional impact. This may involve call history, variations in remuneration, in-app communications, performance alerts, criteria disclosed or omitted, restriction records, rating patterns and comparative data on the change in the environment. There are, here, recurrent blind spots that need to be avoided. The first is to treat fluctuation in earnings as a pure natural risk of the activity, when it may stem from an opaque unilateral reconfiguration of the distribution infrastructure. The second is to treat the final sanction as an isolated event, without reconstructing the regime of conduct, incentive and threat that preceded it. The third is to accept the lack of transparency about metrics and criteria as an inevitable consequence of technology, when precisely this opacity is part of the central legal problem.

The possible dogmatic consequence, in this subtype, tends to gravitate around an abusive practice by structural opacity, qualified informational insufficiency, a defect of the productive supply regime and the unlawfulness of functionally degrading changes when not accompanied by compatible restoration. In borderline cases, especially when the combination of mutability, metrics, sanctions and restrictions reveals a stable program of normalizing losses and capturing conduct, there may be room for a reading in the key of abusive teleology. The most adequate institutional response will tend to favor preservation and disclosure of minimum records, duties of verifiable reasoning, review of restriction criteria, intelligibility about relevant parameters of distribution of opportunities and functional restoration of the regime whenever the platform has degraded, by design, the productive utility it offered as infrastructure.

This incidence does not dissolve the subtype into undifferentiated labor law, but neither does it allow itself to be neutralized by contractual self-descriptions of formal autonomy. The IOC regime makes it possible to capture precisely the zone in which the platform supplies a governed productive environment and thereby comes to organize access, permanence, visibility, intelligibility and contestation in economically relevant terms. It is at this point that iFood and 99Food, on the one hand, and Uber and 99, on the other, cease to be merely delivery or mobility apps and reveal themselves as private infrastructures of economic possibility. When this infrastructure is offered under opacity, unilateral mutability and concentrated sanctioning governance, the problem is no longer <1>p. 769</1> merely contractual nor merely technological. It is a problem of institutional controllability of supply in a context of productive dependence.
