The competition-law incidence of the typology of the Immaterial Object of Consumption does not stem from an external thematic graft, but from the very logic of the governed supply regime. When the platform administers visibility, access, comparability and intelligibility within the ecosystem, it organizes not only the enjoyment of the end user. It also organizes, in a materially relevant way, the conditions under which economic agents compete for attention, preference, trust and conversion within the environment. Competition, in this context, does not appear as a problem separate from consumption, but as an institutional continuation of the same governance of enjoyment already described in the preceding items. The platform that governs the user's experience governs, at the same time, the perceptible field in which competition becomes possible, legible and economically effective.

This rapprochement finds solid grounding in the reading of Daniel Firmato<1><2>816</2></1> de Almeida Glória, for whom competition protection and consumer protection do not constitute autonomous or rival ends, but instruments aimed at shaping a transparent, healthy, harmonious and fair market, in which plurality of suppliers, freedom of choice, respect for the consumer and quality of products and services are kept in balanced tension with economic freedom <3>Glória</3><4>(Glória, 2003, p. 131)</4>.

This perspective makes it possible to understand that competition matters here not as a discipline foreign to the IOC, but because the preservation of real choice, meaningful plurality and legibility of the market is part of the very protection of enjoyment under the CDC. If competition, in this key, is not an end in itself, but an instrument for protecting an uncaptured environment of choice, then the architectural governance of the platform, when it distorts the field of choice, already acquires competition relevance from within the consumer experience itself.

This conclusion is reinforced by the centrality that Glória attributes to freedom of choice and to information as the common core between competition and consumer protection. The author states that the consumer's freedom of choice constitutes the primordial point of all <1>p. 770</1> competition law and that such freedom brings with it information as a guiding principle, because whoever does not know is not truly free to choose <2>Glória</2><3>(Glória, 2003, p. 113)</3>.

In platform ecosystems, this formulation gains new density. The platform does not merely offer alternatives. It produces, through interface, curation, <1>ranking</1>, recommendation, highlighting, reputation and the semantics of the environment, the conditions under which these alternatives can be perceived as real, comparable or preferable. The competition problem, therefore, is no longer reduced to the formal presence of multiple agents in the market. It comes to involve the way in which the perceptible market itself is administered by whoever controls the infrastructure of appearance.

It is precisely for this reason that the competition reading needs to reject the so-called myth of competition, that is, the idea that the mere apparent multiplicity of options would be enough to guarantee factual freedom of choice. Glória observes that the existence of possibilities of option does not mean, by itself, real freedom for the consumer, especially when products, services and contractual clauses present themselves under a homogeneity capable of obscuring effectively distinct alternatives <1>Glória</1><2>(Glória, 2003, p. 115-116)</2>. On platforms, this warning becomes even more serious.

Homogenization does not occur only on the plane of the product or the contract. It may be produced by the governance of the interface itself, when the environment artificially brings certain offers closer, renders others invisible, shifts what is sponsored into the zone of the apparently organic, manipulates comparability and administers the user's perception of what is worth more, appears more or seems more reliable. The illusion of plurality may thus coexist with severe compression of the real conditions of choice.

The consequence is that the governance of enjoyment also comes to have a competition function. When the platform ranks, recommends, highlights, integrates logistically, certifies reputations, sets parameters of appearance and gathers intelligence about the behavior of users and suppliers, it ceases to be merely the environment in which competition takes place. It becomes an agent of its material shaping. In markets of this nature, internal preferencing, self-preferencing, informational barriers, capture of competitive intelligence and opaque discrimination do not necessarily depend on ostensive acts of exclusion. They may operate through structural micro-advantages, produced by the continuous administration of the visibility, comparability and intelligibility of the ecosystem.

The platform does not need to formally expel a competitor to restrict its competitiveness. It is enough to govern the perceptible field asymmetrically, making certain <1>p. 771</1> offers more legible, more reliable, faster, more highlighted or more “natural” in the user's eyes.

At this point, Glória's contribution allows a particularly happy seam between consumer and competition. The author maintains that, in a market deformed by oligopolies, cartels and dominant positions, the consumer's vulnerability intensifies because their freedom is compromised and, at times, they have no choice but to contract with the supplier that dominates the economic sector exploited <1>Glória</1><2>(Glória, 2003, p. 106)</2>. On platforms, this logic reappears in reconfigured form. The dominant position does not always manifest itself as a classic monopoly over a physical good or as an explicit cartel among traditional companies. It may manifest itself as dominance over the private infrastructure that organizes the encounter between user and market. The consumer continues to see “several options”, but the practical conditions of appearance, comparison and selection of these options have already been shaped by the agent that governs the environment. Freedom of choice does not formally disappear. It is administered.

This shift is central to the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>. The platform does not control only a distribution channel. It controls the practical semantics of competition within the environment. It defines, or at least strongly conditions, which competitors will be visible, on what terms they will be compared, under what reputation signals they will appear, what kind of friction they will suffer, what strategic data will be extracted from their activity and how the user will perceive the very space of choice. To that extent, competition ceases to be merely a relation between suppliers and comes to depend on the private architecture of the ecosystem. The governance of enjoyment and the governance of competition overlap. The same mechanism that affects the consumer's experience also affects the concrete freedom to compete of the economic agents that depend on the platform to appear, sell, circulate or reach an audience.

The problem is not to reconstruct here the entire theory of infringements of the economic order. The problem is to establish reading parameters for situations in which the platform, by governing enjoyment, also comes to govern the perceptible conditions of competition. The question becomes less the exhaustive definition of the competition infringement and more the requirement of institutional controllability over mechanisms of visibility, comparison, ranking, prioritization and strategic use of ecosystem data. In this key, the IOC regime does not replace competition law. It provides an entry grammar for understanding when the architecture of the consumer's experience has already become, simultaneously, the architecture of competitive advantage.

<1>p. 772</1> It is at this point that the parameters presented earlier acquire a specific competition function. Open auditability applies as a requirement of minimum intelligibility over relevant criteria of <2>ranking</2>, highlighting, recommendation, preferencing, economic moderation of the environment and possible use of strategic data obtained from the intermediation itself. Without this, the platform governs competition from self-legitimated obscurity, turning opacity into structural advantage. Functional value equivalence, in turn, makes it possible to control rule changes that, without formally excluding certain agents, relevantly downgrade their practical position in the ecosystem, emptying the utility of competitive permanence under the pretext of updating, optimization or change of internal policy. Semiotic vulnerability helps explain why competitive harm also passes through the private administration of the user's perception. And abusive teleology appears when the design of the environment ceases merely to organize circulation and comes to programmatically exploit the gatekeeper position to extract competitive advantage from the very power to govern the perceptible market.

From this, the link between competition protection and consumer protection ceases to seem a rhetorical rapprochement. One protection came to be seen as a corollary of the other, but both walk together as legal guideposts of the market, precisely to correct deformations produced by economic power and by the corrosion of free competition <1>Glória</1><2>(Glória, 2003, p. 2; p. 129)</2>. This fits precisely with the reality of platforms. When the platform controls the environment of circulation and competition, consumer protection cannot be limited to the final object acquired or to the final content displayed. It must reach the way in which the market itself is privately and architecturally produced. Otherwise, consumer protection would remain blind to the mechanism that manufactures, behind the appearance of plurality, the material conditions of reduced choice and compressed competition.

The perspective also makes it possible to refine the institutional reach of consumer choice. Competition is only fully justified when it prevents price setting, the supply of goods and economic power from being at the mercy of structural abuses, preserving a market in which the consumer is effectively the central character, and not a mere residual recipient of the effects of economic domination <1>Glória</1><2>(Glória, 2003, p. 78; p. 118)</2>. In platform ecosystems, this centrality requires understanding that the consumer no longer stands only before competing economic agents. They stand before a private organizer of the competitive arena itself. It is this structural mediation that lowers the usefulness of purely formal traditional categories. The consumer suffers not only when a dominant agent ostensibly excludes rivals. They also suffer when the architecture of the environment <3>p. 773</3> silently reduces comparability, obscures alternatives, normalizes induced preferences and turns choice into a previously preselected path.

The possible institutional consequence is not to assert that every intermediation problem is automatically resolved by the CDC, nor that all interface governance constitutes, by itself, a competition infringement. Whenever the platform, in organizing enjoyment, also comes to organize in an opaque and asymmetric way the perceptible conditions of competition within the ecosystem, there must be a requirement of controllability compatible with the dual dimension of the problem. This means, at a minimum, minimum auditability over relevant ranking criteria, intelligibility about highlighting and preferencing practices, control of changes that deform the functional equivalence of competitive permanence and a non-naive reading of the use of data obtained through the very position of intermediation. The IOC regime, to this extent, does not absorb antitrust, but prevents architecturally governed competition from remaining invisible to the dogmatics of consumption.

The result is a thesis modest in formal competition ambition, but strong in material reach. The platform that governs visibility, access and intelligibility also governs the arena in which consumers choose and competitors compete. In this arena, freedom of choice may be preserved, compressed or theatricalized. Plurality may be real or merely scenic. Comparison may be enlightening or administered. Competition, then, can no longer be thought of only on the plane of the abstract structure of the market, but also on the plane of experience concretely mediated by architecture. It is at this point that the <1>Lex </1> <2>Plataformae</2> reveals its most sensitive dimension. By governing enjoyment, it comes to govern competition without needing to name it as such. The work of Law, here, is precisely to make this governance institutionally visible and controllable.

The author is widely known as Daniel Firmato; however, the cataloging record of his work expressly indicates Glória as the last surname, which is why, in this thesis, in respect for the ABNT standard and the formal pattern required, the author will be referred to by that surname and not by the more popular one. <1>↩</1>

The clearest institutional consequence of the applied typology is the passage from the individually perceived conflict to the injury structurally produced by the supply regime. In platform-governed ecosystems, opacity does not operate merely as an episodic difficulty of proof, nor does mutability appear merely as a scattered contractual inconvenience. When the absence of verifiable trails, the adoption of non-auditable change regimes and the opaque administration of sanctions, priorities and reconfigurations become ordinary elements of the environment, the problem ceases to be adequately understood as a sum of isolated harms. What emerges is a form of injury that projects itself onto the very <1>p. 774</1> controllability of enjoyment. It is at this point that collective redress ceases to be a mere procedural convenience and imposes itself as a coherent dogmatic consequence of the IOC regime.

The basis of collective redress, here, lies not only in the circumstance that many consumers may be affected by similar facts. This finding, although relevant, would still remain too dependent on a quantitative logic. The central point is another. In platform environments, the harmful source may reside in the very design of the supply regime, so that the unity of the problem does not stem primarily from the empirical repetition of episodes, but from the permanence of a single, repeatable and functionally expansive structure producing loss, opacity and asymmetry. The injury, then, is not merely plural. It is architectural. It arises from the way the environment was organized to govern enjoyment, administer the intelligibility of the bond and selectively distribute the conditions of evidence, reaction and restoration.

That is why one may speak, in this context, of architecture harm. The expression does not refer to a simple technical defect of the system nor to a metaphorical category intended to embellish the argument. It refers to an injury produced by the very design of the supply regime, and therefore endowed with sufficient functional unity to justify collective institutional treatment. When the platform structures the environment so as to make relevant changes unverifiable, to obscure the relation between promise and delivery, to hinder reconstruction of sanctions, to volatilize essential records or to govern the experience by criteria whose intelligibility remains selectively concentrated, the injury is not limited to the consumer who first manages to perceive it or litigate it. It affects the very collective possibility of controlling enjoyment. The harm, thus, is not only to the individual result of consumption. It is to the institutional verifiability of supply.

This formulation is important because it prevents two recurrent errors. The first is reducing collective redress to a mechanism for aggregating individual claims, as if its function were only to make more efficient the handling of multiple similar event-harms. The second is inflating the structural discourse without demonstrating to what extent the unity of the problem stems from the very governance of the ecosystem. The parameter adopted here avoids both. Collective redress is justified when the harmful source remains unitary, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary functioning of the platform. In this case, the problem lies not only in the quantitative repetition of the harm, but in the qualitative stability of the arrangement that produces it. Repeated opacity, persistent absence of history and non-auditable mutability together form a regime defect.

<1>p. 775</1> This reading follows directly from the centrality of open auditability in the IOC regime. If the controllability of enjoyment depends on minimum institutional intelligibility about changes, sanctions, presentation criteria, distribution mechanisms and other relevant aspects of the governed experience, then the systematic absence of these conditions already constitutes an injury that goes beyond the sphere of the single case. It is not merely a matter of saying that a consumer was left without sufficient evidence. It is a matter of recognizing that the environment was structured to make precarious, at scale, the possibility of reconstructing the bond. The problem, in this scenario, belongs to the architecture of supply, and not merely to the unhappy luck of a specific user. The insufficiency of verifiable trails ceases to be an accidental procedural obstacle and becomes a mode of operation of the ecosystem.

The institutional consequence of this is clear. When the platform organizes supply under recurrent patterns of structural opacity, protection cannot settle for strictly retrospective and individualized remedies. Correction must reach the regime. Collective redress then proves particularly suited to impose injunctive, procedural and analytical measures capable of reintroducing institutional verifiability into the environment. This may involve duties to preserve minimum records, a requirement of verifiable reasoning for materially relevant sanctions, maintenance of an accessible history of relevant changes, explanation of minimum operational criteria of distribution, priority or ranking, and other measures aimed not only at repairing past harms, but at reorganizing the future conditions of controllability of enjoyment.

This corrective vocation is especially important because, in governed ecosystems, the repetition of the injury does not depend on an identical reiteration of external facts. It stems from the permanence of the same private decision structure. An opaque sanctions policy, a non-auditable regime of functional change, an interface logic that dilutes the essential under informational excess, a materially decisive ranking system without usable history or a trust architecture that absorbs and neutralizes contestation before it becomes litigation are all examples of problems whose unity lies in the design, not in the episode. The legal system loses responsiveness when it tries to treat each manifestation of this pattern as an isolated fact. Collective redress, on the contrary, makes it possible to bring the manifestations back to their unitary source.

This does not mean abolishing the role of individual protection. It remains indispensable, above all for the reparation of concretely experienced losses and for the situated reconstruction of certain specific impacts. What is asserted is that, when the litigation reveals a structural pattern of opacity, absence of trails, degrading mutability or non-auditable sanction, the <1>p. 776</1> adequate institutional response cannot be exhausted on the individual plane. Merely atomized treatment of the conflict tends to produce two bad results. On the one hand, it monetizes episodes without altering the machine that reproduces them. On the other, it transforms the systemic difficulty of proof into the private failure of dispersed consumers, each obliged to face alone an informational regime designed precisely to hinder reconstruction. Collective redress corrects both deviations, because it shifts the focus from the event-harm to the governance that makes it normal.

The notion of architecture harm further helps to understand why the indivisibility of the injury does not depend only on a material community of losses, but on the functional unity of the aggressing source. When the platform operates under the same opaque regime for all users inserted in a given dynamic of enjoyment, the collective injury may reside precisely in the common subjection to an environment whose verifiability has been structurally compromised. The impact is not homogeneous in all its effects, but it is common in its matrix. All users are inserted into an ecosystem that asymmetrically distributes meaning, evidence and capacity for contestation. The collective injury, then, is not limited to the final content of each one's loss. It bears on the very level of institutional controllability of the supply regime.

It is at this point that open auditability turns from a dogmatic standard into a condition of effectiveness of collective redress. Without it, the action of parties with collective standing, administrative protection bodies and regulatory and supervisory structures tends to run into the same opacity that already hinders individual reaction. With it, it becomes possible to transform the requirement of verifiability into the main object of protection, shifting the debate from isolated episodes to the shaping of the environment. Collective redress then comes to operate not only as a response to consummated harms, but as an institutional technology for reintroducing intelligibility, preserving evidence and containing private regimes that remain functionally impenetrable.

If the typical models analyzed demonstrate that the platform governs enjoyment through recurrent mechanisms of visibility, opacity, mutability, sanction and administration of trust, then the institutional response cannot remain confined to the horizon of the single lawsuit. The typology reveals precisely that certain harms are programmatic. Not because all cases are the same, but because the source of their production remains structurally the same. In these contexts, collective redress does not represent an expansionist deviation of the CDC. It represents the adequate way of treating injuries whose dogmatic unity is already given by the architecture of supply.

<1>p. 777</1> The result is a strong institutional conclusion, but a methodologically restrained one. The repetition of structural opacity, the persistent absence of verifiable trails and the adoption of non-auditable regimes of change and sanction naturally lead to structural injuries typical of collective redress because they make the very controllability of enjoyment a legally affected interest. What is protected, then, is not only the patrimony or the individual experience of dispersed consumers, but the institutional integrity of the conditions under which enjoyment can be understood, proven, contested and restored. When the private supply regime compromises these conditions on an architectural scale, the legal response must be equally capable of reaching the architecture. Otherwise, the system merely tallies harms while opacity keeps producing them in silence.

The incidence of the CDC in platform ecosystems requires a functional reading of the relationship, capable of going beyond contractual self-descriptions that, although formally elegant, are materially insufficient to explain the real supply regime. In environments governed by private architecture, the dispute is not adequately resolved by the simple question of who acquires what at the end of the chain, nor by the isolated verification of professionalism, economic instrumentality or peripheral insertion of the subject in the ecosystem. The decisive fact lies in the way the environment concentrates power, organizes asymmetry of meaning, produces evidentiary asymmetry and administers the very conditions of access, permanence, visibility, verification and contestation. Whenever this functional subjection proves legally relevant, the neutralization of consumer-law protection by civil appearances of parity must be rejected.

This point is especially important because platforms frequently operate through strategies of formal mischaracterization of the relationship. In some cases, they present themselves as mere neutral infrastructure for the encounter of autonomous parties. In others, they qualify the relationship as business collaboration, technological partnership, pure intermediation or simple licensing of access to a tool. In all these arrangements, contractual vocabulary tends to shift attention from the effective governance regime to the symmetrical appearance of the contractual frame. The dogmatic problem, however, lies not in the drafting sophistication of the contract, but in the materiality of the subjection produced by the ecosystem. When the platform concentrates the power to modulate enjoyment, to redistribute informational risks, to govern evidence and to condition the <1>p. 778</1> continuity of the subject's insertion in the environment, formal parity comes to have limited explanatory value.

It is in this context that deepened finalism appears here as a reading criterion and not as an autonomous object of doctrinal exposition. Its usefulness lies in preventing the figure of the consumer from being compressed by an excessively narrow reading of the final recipient, incapable of capturing relationships in which vulnerability stems less from the classic position in the economic chain and more from submission to a private environment of concentrated governance. The focus, therefore, is not on indiscriminately inflating the concept of consumer, but on preventing the dogmatics of continuous supply from being neutralized by formal classifications that ignore who effectively bears the architecture of risk, opacity and functional dependence. In ecosystems of this nature, vulnerability does not dissolve because the subject earns income, uses the platform to make their activity viable or presents themselves, to some extent, as an economically active agent. What matters is whether they remain subject, in asymmetric terms, to the private regime that organizes meaning, visibility, permanence and evidence.

This key is particularly relevant for reaching situations in which <1>sellers</1>, partners, productive users of infrastructure and other participants economically inserted in the environment remain exposed to the platform's unilateral governance to a degree materially incompatible with a simple presumption of parity. The <2>seller</2> who depends on ranking, reputation, visibility and opaque prioritization rules does not become immune to consumer-law protection merely because they sell. The partner who uses the infrastructure to produce income does not cease to be vulnerable merely because they earn revenue. The peripheral professionalized user does not automatically become the strong party to the relationship just because their activity has an economic purpose. In all these cases, the legally relevant question lies in the density of the platform's governance over their insertion in the ecosystem. If permanence, the intelligibility of the environment, the reconstruction of the conflict and the contestation of relevant decisions remain concentrated under the platform's private control, the a priori exclusion of the CDC by formal label loses adherence.

That is why functional exposure to governance practices and semiotic vulnerability must be treated here as central dimensions of factual vulnerability. The subject is not vulnerable only because they know less or because they have lower abstract economic capacity. They are vulnerable because they are inserted in an environment that produces the very legibility of the relationship, defines the criteria of internal relevance, administers the signals of trust, controls the records of what occurred and concentrates the power to change the conditions of enjoyment. On platforms, asymmetry is not limited to the content of the contract. It projects itself onto the way <1>p. 779</1> in which the reality of the bond can be perceived, narrated and proven. This form of vulnerability reaches not only the classic consumer, but also other subjects functionally exposed to the concentrated governance of the ecosystem.

The usefulness of Article 29 of the CDC<1><2>817</2></1> then appears with special force. Its functional reading makes it possible to reach cases in which the subject, although not fitting comfortably into the traditional figure of the final acquirer as imagined in linear and simple relationships, finds themselves exposed to the commercial practices, supply methods and private governance mechanisms of the environment in a condition of legally relevant vulnerability. The point is not to dissolve every distinction between consumer and economic agent. It is to recognize that, in governed ecosystems, functional exposure to platform practices may produce situations in which consumer-law protection remains justified even when the relationship does not fit, without effort, into the classic photograph of private domestic consumption. Dogmatics must be able to see the structure before deciding on exclusion.

This reading also prevents peripheral professionalization from being used as a universal screen against the CDC. In many platform environments, the subject may carry out their own economic activity, minimally organize their routine, earn income and still remain dependent on a private infrastructure they do not control, whose criteria of visibility, sanction, prioritization and evidence remain opaque and unilaterally modulable. There is no contradiction in this. The existence of the user's economic interest does not, by itself, eliminate the vulnerability arising from the governance of the ecosystem. The error would lie in presuming that any productive insertion automatically transforms structural asymmetry into a relationship between equals. On platforms, this presumption is frequently misleading precisely because the appearance of autonomy coexists with severe concentration of private power over the real conditions of operation.

The dogmatic consequence of this framing is important. The CDC may apply not only where there is a classic final acquisition, but also where the platform produces relevant functional subjection to a private governance environment that administers, in concentrated form, <1>p. 780</1> access, permanence, visibility, verifiability and contestation. In these cases, the consumer by equivalence does not arise as a figure artificially expanded by theoretical generosity. It arises as a necessary response to supply models that have shifted the center of vulnerability into the architecture of the environment. The question then ceases to be whether the subject is “too much of a businessperson” to deserve protection and becomes whether the relationship, as structured, remains marked by material asymmetry of power and by submission to legally controllable private governance.

This does not authorize indiscriminate inflation of the category. The criterion remains demanding. Not every participant in a platform ecosystem will be a consumer by equivalence. Not every relationship economically mediated by technology will justify the incidence of the CDC. What is asserted is something more delimited and more serious. When the platform organizes the very intelligibility of the bond, concentrates the evidence of what it does, opaquely distributes opportunities and risks and conditions the continuity of the subject's insertion in the environment, the automatic exclusion of consumer-law protection by reference to nominal appearances of professionalism or partnership becomes methodologically poor and normatively dangerous. What decides is the real structure of subjection, not the contractual appearance of horizontality.

In this key, coherence is preserved with the constitutional matrix and with the functional reading of Article 29 of the CDC. Protection does not move beyond the system. On the contrary, it emerges from the very need to prevent new regimes of continuous and governed supply from escaping control by means of private vocabularies that simulate parity where there is dependence, simulate neutrality where there is concentrated management and simulate simple intermediation where there is effective unilateral organization of the experience. Deepened finalism, here, does not enter as a lecture. It enters as a tool to prevent dogmatic blindness before ecosystems in which vulnerability no longer presents itself in the classic garb of consumption, but remains perfectly alive under the logic of the platform.
